newsitem.title: UK: Gene delays AIDS but hastens death - study.
newsitem.headline: Gene delays AIDS but hastens death - study.

text.p: A genetic mutation that helps some HIV-infected people resist AIDS causes a quicker death once they do develop the infection, Danish doctors said on Friday.
Some people have a slightly different version of a cell receptor -- a kind of doorway -- known as CCR5. It is one receptor used by the HIV virus to hijack cells.
This variation makes it a little harder for the virus to infect cells, so these people are HIV-infected but slower to develop the diseases that mark full-blown Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.
But Dr Peter Garred and colleagues at the Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen said this advantage did not last long.
"The protective effect of the (mutation) lasted for about seven years," they wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.

Early on in the infection, those with the mutation had much higher CD4 counts -- a measure of immune system cells and thus of immune system strength -- than most HIV-infected people at the same stage.
"However, this picture was reversed when AIDS was diagnosed," Garred's group wrote. They said the reason was not yet clear.
